messages.body_plain:
I really don't know. I have doubts about whether local capture-recapture data can be modelled adequately to adjust for losses due to long-distance dispersal. On the other hand, we have submitted some work that suggests robustness to misspecification of the dispersal model. I cannot say how this applies in your case, and I doubt there are general answers. The way forward is probably to confirm model behaviour by simulating your particular scenario, which I know would be a burden. Richard Glennie's software openpopscr on GiTHub is an alternative that does not require truncation of the kernel at a pre-determined radius, but that may fail to deal with long-distance dispersal (fat tails) because it is limited to bivariate normal kernels.
Murray

messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I was wondering whether there is any way to add in some extra parameters that I would like estimated in the userdist function?
As a simple example, using simply the mask I would like to estimate the cost of traversing an NA cell. I would like to do the following in my userdist function:

userdfn2 <- function (xy1, xy2, mask) {
  if (missing(xy1)) return("noneuc","c")
  require(gdistance)
  Sraster <- raster(mask, "noneuc")

   # Assume animals can traverse gaps: bridge gaps using an estimated value
  Sraster[is.na <http://is.na>(Sraster[])] <- c

  # conductance is inverse of friction
  trans <- transition(Sraster, transitionFunction = function(x) 1/mean(x),
                      directions = 16)
  trans <- geoCorrection(trans)
  costDistance(trans, as.matrix(xy1), as.matrix(xy2))
}

I am would like to try to emulate landscape resistance optimization as in the ResistanceGA R package but for SECR models.
The ResistanceGA package uses a gravity model and directly estimates the cost of each pixel using genetic distance between individuals or populations and landscape covariates in raster format.
For a continuous surface such as a DEM, the cost of elevation is estimated from 3 parameters that transform the values of the DEM.
However, for a binary surface such as the one above, the only parameter to estimate is the cost value of the most costly feature (the NA areas).

Is this at all possible right now in SECR?

Thanks!

Robby

messages.subject: Re: openCR age modelling
messages.body_plain:
openCR.fit() automatically applies join() if the capthist input has a multi-session structure. It doesn't work any differently for age models, and you should get the same result by applying join() yourself. I would be interested if you can provide a simple working example where it has an effect. Perhaps there is some subtle difference in the specification of intervals, or the dots argument of your call to openCR.fit() is passing something unintended to join().
Murray

messages.body_plain:
Interesting, but I'm not sure I have the picture.

In secr-noneuclidean.pdf <https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/pdfs/secr-noneuclidean.pdf> I read "noneuc’ has its own link scale (default ‘log’) on which it may be modelled as a linear function of anyof the predictors available for density (x, y, x2, y2, xy, session, Session, g, or any mask covariate – see secr-densitysurfaces.pdf)... When the model is fitted by secr.fit, the beta parameters for the ‘noneuc’submodel are estimated along with all the others. To make noneuc available to userdist, ensure that it appears in the ‘model’ argument. Use the formula noneuc ~ 1 if noneuc is constant."

So the coefficients of the linear model for noneuc are 'extra parameters' that might conceivably do the job. I take it you would like to escape the linear model formalism and estimate 3 parameters (coefficients) that are unmodelled (constant across space, time etc.). There is an undocumented feature in secr.fit that allows up to 4 unmodelled parameters, but these are presently not passed to userdist. This could be fixed.

Murray

messages.body_plain:
After more investigation - I'm happy with the way the software works. It's not obvious what levels predict() should generate automatically for time-varying trap covariates, so it's up to you to specify them in newdata. Also, be sure you really want to use a covariate rather than specifying effort via usage().

> > userdfn2 <- function (xy1, xy2, mask) {
> >   if (missing(xy1)) return("noneuc","c")

> I've been running some trials with various variance estimators, weighted and unweighted. The major results are as expected
> - if you have large-scale variation in density across your study area then assuming Poisson n causes the sampling variance (se(D-hat) to be underestimated
> - 'empirical' estimates of var(n) by any of the methods (Poisson, weighted or unweighted) are OK (slightly +ve bias of se(D-hat) ) as long as the population is uniformly distributed and clusters are located as a simple random sample
> - placing clusters systematically (with random origin) was more efficient than a random sample when density was NOT uniform, but none of the present 'empirical' estimators captured this benefit (i.e. se(D-hat) was overestimated). Good day,

I've got some comparative estimates of density with confidence limits from sets of study areas ("traplines") within larger areas of interest (WLZs).
Recall that the spatial configuration of traplines varies, and that we were also concerned about variation in detection parameters among traplines.
Samples from all traplines should be adequate (30 - 60 animals, 3-4 detections per animal on average, plenty of spatial recaptures).
Estimates of sigma are consistent with independent information about sex-specific home range sizes, but variable.

I'd previously completed analyses of trapline-specific data to estimate density in the vicinity of each trapline.
Point estimates of density from different traplines in one WLZ (top figure, 5 traplines) were fairly similar (range 0.00038 - 0.00083 / ha).
Those in the other WLZ were more variable (range 0.00034 - 0.0018 / ha, where the highest estimate was more than double any of the other estimates).

messages.subject_clean: Discrepancies between secr and openCR estimates for closed pop. models
messages.body_plain:
Using both my own data and a test dataset, there appears to be some pretty big discrepancies between parameter estimates for, as far as I can tell, the same closed population model using secr.fit and openCR.fit packages.

Using the OVpossumCH dataset as an example:

# load data etc
ovtrap <- traps(OVpossumCH[[1]])
datadir <- system.file("extdata", package = "secr")
OVforest <- rgdal::readOGR(dsn = datadir, layer = "OVforest")
ovmask <- make.mask(ovtrap, buffer = 120, type = 'trapbuffer', poly = OVforest[1:2,], spacing = 15, keep.poly = FALSE)
intervals(OVpossumCH) <- c(123, 91, 154, 118, 85)/365 # annual

# fit closed pop model using opencr
closed_opencr <- openCR.fit(OVpossumCH, mask = ovmask, detectfn = "HHR", type = 'secrD')
# massage the predict.openCR results to the same format as predict.secr
pred_closed_opencr <- plyr::rbind.fill(predict(closed_opencr))[c(2,1,3),-1]
rownames(pred_closed_opencr) <- secr$realnames

# fit closed pop model using secr
closed_secr <- secr.fit(OVpossumCH, mask = ovmask, detectfn = "HHR")

# compare the estimates
predict(closed_secr).
pred_closed_opencr

closed_secr gives a D estimate of: 10.1187047
closed_opencr gives a D estimate of: 14.2337598

The difference is much greater in my own dataset.
Perhaps I am I missing something obvious (wouldn't be the first time...) - are these models not doing the same thing?

Any thoughts would be greatly appreciated group/Murray!

Cheers,
Matt.

closed_secr1 <- secr.fit(OVpossumCH[[1]], mask = ovmask, detectfn = "HHR")

messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I am aware there is a separate Google Group for oSCR, but I haven't been able to get access to the oSCR group, so I am positing here. I have a large SCR dataset, and I'm using the latest version ( 0.42.0) of the package oSCR to analyze these data with hopes of producing density weighted connectivity estimates. I have 1914 trap locations, 303 individuals and 425 spatial detections. Thus the state-space is quite large

I am using the oscr.fit function to fit models and get default starting values for my parameters, but this has proven challenging so far. I was able to successfully fit a null model, which took about 8 hours to run with this dataset. I am now trying to run detection sub-models. However, whenever I add covariates on detection (p0) and use default starting values provided by the oscr.fit function the models run initially, but then fail after several hours or even days, with the error message: warning ( "Something went wrong! Try better starting values.")

I have double checked my scr.Frame, and checked to make sure that all covariates are scaled and/or centered. I have both continuous covariates and binary covariates (e.g., 1 or 0 representing the trap type). I reduced my UTM coordinates to kilometers as well. I don't get any errors or warnings with oSCR functions, including oscr.fit prior to actual model fitting, so I am somewhat stumped on what is going wrong here. I have started to comb through the source code for oscr.fit, but I can't quite untangle the syntax to understand what is happening mathematically when the models fail at this stage.

What I did notice was the oscr.fit (get starts = T) returns a default starting value of 0 for all of the covariates on p0, which seems uninformative. Currently I am experimenting with replacing those 0's with a more informative starting value based on general hypotheses, e.g. an increase in forest cover increases probability of detection to see if this could possibly help with model convergence.

Any insight would be greatly appreciated!

- Sarah
